chapters.title: Your liver turns sugar into fat
Your teeth and the WHO limit
The best news: how fast your body recovers

scenes.text: One can of soda can hold more sugar than the World Health Organization's ideal limit for an entire day.

items.label: WHO ideal limit for a whole day

scenes.text: So what actually happens inside your body when all that sugar goes down?
I'll take you through four places sugar hits, one by one, and the last part of this video is the best news most people never hear.
First, a quick truth: sugar itself isn't poison. Your body runs on glucose. The problem is how much, and how fast.
Number one: your blood.
Table sugar is half glucose and half fructose. Minutes after a sweet drink, glucose floods into your bloodstream.
Liquid sugar is the fastest. There's no fibre to slow it down, so your blood sugar rises in a sharp spike.
Your pancreas answers with insulin, the hormone that works like a key, unlocking your cells so glucose can get in and be used for energy.
Do this once, and your body handles it well. Do it every day, and your cells can slowly stop listening to insulin.
That's called insulin resistance, and it's the road that leads to type 2 diabetes.
In a review of eight studies and over three hundred thousand people, those who drank one to two sugary drinks a day had a twenty six percent higher risk of type 2 diabetes.
And this matters close to home. A national study in India of over one hundred thousand people found eleven point four percent have diabetes, and another fifteen point three percent have prediabetes.
Number two: your liver.
Glucose can be used by almost every cell in your body. Fructose is different. Most of it travels straight to your liver.
When your liver gets more fructose than it needs, it does something clever and dangerous: it turns the extra into fat. Doctors call it de novo lipogenesis, which means making new fat.
Some of that fat stays inside the liver. Over time, this is how fatty liver disease can start, even in people who never drink alcohol.

panels.text: Sugary drinks are a major risk factor for fatty liver disease.
panels.source: Softic et al., Digestive Diseases and Sciences 2016

scenes.text: Number three: your heart.
Extra sugar raises the fats in your blood, pushes up your weight, and over the years puts strain on your heart and arteries.
A large American study followed more than eleven thousand adults for almost fifteen years.

panels.source: Yang et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2014

scenes.text: People who got a quarter or more of their calories from added sugar had nearly three times the risk of dying from heart disease, compared with people under ten percent.

panels.caption: Risk of dying from heart disease

panels.label: the risk, at 25%+ of calories from added sugar

scenes.text: And seven in ten adults in that study were already above the ten percent line.

panels.label: of US adults got 10%+ of calories from added sugar

scenes.text: Number four: your teeth.
Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugar and release acid. That acid slowly dissolves your enamel and causes cavities.
This is so well proven that it's one of the main reasons the WHO set its sugar limit: less than ten percent of your daily energy, and ideally under five percent, about six teaspoons.

panels.label: of daily energy: the upper limit

scenes.text: Now compare that with one can of soda: up to ten teaspoons. One drink, and you're past the ideal limit for the whole day.

panels.label: One can of soda: up to 10 teaspoons

panels.text: Past the limit in one drink

scenes.text: And it isn't only soda. One tablespoon of ketchup has about a teaspoon of sugar hiding inside it.

panels.label: 1 tablespoon of ketchup ≈ 1 teaspoon of sugar

scenes.text: But here's the twist: the sugar in a whole apple and the sugar in apple juice are almost the same molecules, yet your body treats them very differently.
A study of more than one hundred eighty thousand people found that eating whole fruits like blueberries, grapes and apples was linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes.
But the same amount of fruit juice was linked to a higher risk. The difference is fibre: whole fruit makes your body work to get the sugar out, so it arrives slowly.
That's why the WHO limit counts fruit juice and honey as free sugar, but not the sugar in fresh whole fruit.

panels.text: Juice and honey count as free sugar. Fresh whole fruit does not.
Eat the fruit. Skip the juice.

scenes.text: And now, the best news I promised you. When researchers swapped sugar for starch in children's meals, keeping calories the same, liver fat dropped from seven point two percent to three point eight percent in just nine days.
Same calories. Just less sugar. Their livers also made far less new fat, and their insulin worked better.

items.label: New fat made by the liver, before

scenes.text: Your body is not stuck. Cut the added sugar, and it starts repairing itself faster than most people expect.
So start simple: swap soda for water or plain milk, eat your fruit instead of drinking it, and check labels for hidden sugar.
Tell me in the comments which of these surprised you most.
Because now you know why one can of soda can hold more sugar than the ideal limit for an entire day, and exactly where all of it goes inside your body.

scenes.text: One can of soda can hold ten teaspoons of sugar.
Here are three things it does inside you, and the last one surprises everyone.
Number one: your blood sugar spikes, because liquid sugar has no fibre to slow it down.
Number two: your pancreas floods your blood with insulin to push that sugar into your cells.
Number three: most of the fructose goes straight to your liver.
But here's the twist: your liver can turn that extra fructose into brand new fat.
The surprise? Cutting added sugar lowered liver fat in children in just nine days.
So, think twice about one can of soda: ten teaspoons of sugar.

scenes.text: Is the sugar in an apple the same as the sugar in apple juice?
Three facts settle it, and the last one changes how you shop.
Number one: both contain the same kinds of sugar, glucose and fructose.
Number two: a whole apple comes with fibre, so your body has to work to release the sugar slowly.
But here's the twist: in a study of over one hundred eighty thousand people, whole fruit was linked to lower diabetes risk, and juice to higher.
Number three: the WHO counts juice as free sugar, but not whole fruit.

panels.text: Whole fruit: not counted. Juice: counted.

scenes.text: So, apple or apple juice? Not the same sugar.

scenes.text: Your liver can start losing fat in just nine days.
Here's how, in three steps, and the last number is the one doctors love.
Number one: researchers kept children's calories exactly the same.
Number two: they only swapped added sugar for starch.
It was a real clinical study, with forty one children aged nine to eighteen, and every single meal was provided.
But here's the twist: they didn't eat less. Same calories, same amount of carbs. The only change was less sugar.
Number three: liver fat fell from seven point two to three point eight percent.
So yes, your liver can start losing fat in just nine days.
